source_text: Et incipere, et bene incipere substantiam, a necessarii unione dirigitur. Accipit etiam arbitrii libertatem; aeque adhuc necessarii linea continetur; sed iam necessariorum finis est; hinc finduntur in contraria voluntates. Ad unionem ergo necessarii divisionis natura non pertinet. Ita possibilitatem habere cogimur; uti autem vel bene vel male ipsa possibilitate non cogimur. Ita fit ut etiam possibilitas peccandi capax boni malique, sed voluntarii sit; quoniam boni proprii capax esse non poterat, nisi capax esset et pravi.
pass_a_gloss: Both to begin, and to begin well a substance, is directed from the union of the necessary. He also receives freedom of decision; equally thus far it is contained by the line of the necessary; but already it is the end of necessary things; from here wills are split into contraries. To the union of the necessary therefore the nature of division does not belong. Thus we are compelled to have a possibility; but we are not compelled to use that possibility itself either well or evilly. Thus it is done that even a possibility of sinning is capable of good and of evil, but of the voluntary; because it could not be capable of its own good, unless it were capable also of the crooked.

lemmas.lexica: LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS libertas; Blaise moral freedom to will or refuse
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: A substance’s beginning, and its good beginning, are governed by the unity of necessity. The human being also receives freedom of will, still within the line of necessity. But here necessary things end; from this point wills divide into opposites. The nature of division does not belong to necessity’s unity. Thus we are compelled to possess the capacity, but not compelled to use that capacity either well or badly. The capacity to sin is therefore capable of good and evil, but voluntary good and evil, because it could not be capable of a person’s own good unless it were capable of wrongdoing too.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
